section_summary: This section assembles wartime reporting and analysis on Japan’s political stability, civilian morale, economic shortages, air raids, shipping losses, communism, parliamentarian traditions, and prospects for postwar government. It includes diplomatic despatches, OSS intelligence, State Department memoranda and cross-references, Soviet press analysis, a German-language newspaper clipping with an English translation, and translations from Chinese Communist publications. The final documents emphasize antiwar sentiment, Soviet-Japanese economic and fisheries agreements, rationing, black markets, and deteriorating living conditions inside Japan.

subfiles.title: A Rumanian Traveler Describes Conditions in Japan Between July 1943 and December 1944
subfiles.from: Burton Y. Berry, United States Representative in Romania
subfiles.about: Reports Edmond Ciuntu’s observations of wartime morale, politics, living conditions, air raids, prisoners, industry, and shipping in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Berry presents Ciuntu as a reliable former Romanian diplomat who lived in Japan from July 1943 until November 1944. Ciuntu describes strong public discipline but elite doubts about victory, growing isolation of foreigners, preparations for American bombing, and reportedly improved treatment of American internees. He also details female industrial mobilization, acute shortages of food, fuel, clothing, paper, and transport, and attributes much of the deterioration to Japanese shipping losses.

subfiles.title: A Rumanian’s Observation of Conditions in Japan
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Romanian civilian’s observations of Japanese morale, air defenses, prisoner treatment, political authority, transportation, and diplomacy.
subfiles.summary: OSS report from a Rumanian: morale high, upper classes doubting victory and hoping for Soviet mediation, calm during November raids, strict travel controls and the Army and Navy dominant.

subfiles.title: Military Defeats Affecting the Japanese Political Situation
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a memorandum concerning how military defeats affected Japan’s political situation.
subfiles.summary: Filing sheet for a memorandum on the political effects of Japanese military defeats; the original is filed elsewhere.

subfiles.title: The Japanese Communist Party
subfiles.about: Records the submission of a memorandum entitled “The Japanese Communist Party.”
subfiles.summary: Sheet pointing to a confidential-file item on the Japanese Communist Party sent from Chungking by Davies.

subfiles.title: Letter Acknowledging Suggested Books
subfiles.about: Thanks the recipient and Grew for suggested titles and mentions study of speeches relating to world order.
subfiles.summary: Poorly legible letter thanking the sender for suggested books, two of which will be ordered.

subfiles.title: Communism and the Future of Japan
subfiles.about: Considers the possible growth of communism in postwar Japan and recommends a firm but culturally influential American policy.
subfiles.summary: Emmerson argues Chinese Communists seek Communist governments in China and Japan; the US should use Japanese Communists for political warfare, encourage broad representation, and open Japan to outside information.

subfiles.title: Letter from the Federal Capital: Japanese Parliamentarianism
subfiles.about: Reviews the history of Japanese constitutional government and proposes restoration of imperial authority as a means of ending military dictatorship.
subfiles.summary: The article traces Japanese parliamentarianism from the 1889 Constitution through party cabinets, military encroachments, assassinations, the Manchurian crisis, and the suppression of political parties. It maintains that genuine parliamentary and democratic currents survived despite military control and cites Grew and numerous Japanese politicians in support. For postwar reconstruction it advocates removing the military government, retaining the emperor as a source of legitimate popular authority, disarming Japan, returning conquered territories, and amending the constitution to prevent independent military policy.

subfiles.title: Brief aus der Bundeshauptstadt: Japanischer Parlamentarismus
subfiles.about: Provides the original German newspaper version of the article translated on pages 13–22.
subfiles.summary: German clipping argues Japanese parliamentary traditions survived military rule and recommends defeating the militarists while keeping the emperor. Adjacent columns are unrelated.

subfiles.title: Correction Concerning the Red Star Article on Japan
subfiles.about: Corrects the publication in which a Soviet article on Japan appeared and announces a forthcoming summary.
subfiles.summary: Harriman corrects that the article appeared in Red Star on February 4, not Pravda; full summary follows.

subfiles.title: Cover Note on the Red Star Analysis of Japan
subfiles.from: B. R. Johansen, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards a telegram and summary concerning a major Red Star article on Japan’s internal politics.
subfiles.summary: Johansen's cover note pointing to the Red Star analysis, Moscow telegram 843 and the State Department comment.

subfiles.title: Japan, Internal Political Situation, as Analyzed in the February 4 Issue of Red Star
subfiles.from: B. R. Johansen, Division of Japanese Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes and evaluates the Soviet claim that military setbacks were reviving less-totalitarian political forces in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Red Star argues Tojo's fall exposed military-fascist weakness; Johansen sees a gain by less-totalitarian elements driven by business resistance, though conditions push toward regimentation.

subfiles.title: Summary of E. Zhukov’s Red Star Article on the Political Situation of Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a detailed summary of a Soviet analysis of political change and declining war support in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The article portrays Tojo’s 1944 resignation as evidence that outright military-fascist dictatorship lacked support even in elite Japanese circles. It reviews failed attempts to replace political parties with throne-assistance organizations and argues that Koiso’s cabinet and the Diet reflected renewed influence by former parliamentary groups. The author nevertheless sees continued strength among reactionary forces while bombing, defeats, food shortages, and manpower strains undermine chauvinistic propaganda and popular support for the war.

subfiles.title: Koiso’s Replies to Questions in Parliament
subfiles.about: Points to Moscow telegram 959 reporting press accounts of Koiso’s parliamentary replies.
subfiles.summary: Filing note for a Moscow telegram on Koiso's answers to questions in Parliament; the telegram is filed elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Translations of Articles from Chinese Communist Publications on Political and Economic Developments in Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards translations of Chinese Communist articles concerning Japan, occupied territories, political leaders, and wartime living conditions.
subfiles.summary: Embassy encloses Yan'an Chinese Communist articles on Soviet-Japanese treaties, Japanese living conditions, Philippine independence, Luzon, the Koiso cabinet and profiles of Yoshida Shigeru and Ando Riki.

subfiles.title: Defeatism in Japan
subfiles.from: Coordinated Translation Center, Chungking; original article by Pu I in Liberation Daily
subfiles.to: Office of War Information; information copies to OSS and American Embassy
subfiles.about: Presents a Chinese Communist interpretation of growing defeatism, antiwar sentiment, cultural dissent, and ideological repression in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Translated article on defeatism in Japan: sabotage, hoarding and open dissatisfaction with militarism; Ozaki's arrest and Kaji's denunciation show repression, while opposition could form an anti-fascist front.

subfiles.title: Two Treaties Recently Signed Between the Soviet Union and Japan
subfiles.from: Coordinated Translation Center, Chungking; original article in Liberation Daily
subfiles.to: Office of War Information; information copies to OSS and American Embassy
subfiles.about: Analyzes Soviet-Japanese agreements over northern Sakhalin concessions and fisheries as a Soviet diplomatic victory.
subfiles.summary: Translated article on two Soviet-Japanese treaties: northern Sakhalin concessions, fisheries disputes since 1936, and new agreements forcing Japanese concessions.

subfiles.title: Round Table Conference on the Living Conditions of the Japanese People
subfiles.from: Coordinated Translation Center, Chungking; original in Liberation Daily
subfiles.to: Office of War Information; information copies to Far Eastern Affairs, OSS, and American Embassy
subfiles.about: Records testimony about wartime Japanese rationing, black markets, food scarcity, tobacco, clothing, and household goods.
subfiles.summary: Participants compare local rice allowances and describe irregular supplies of fish, meat, vegetables, salt, bean paste, sugar, alcohol, fruit, tobacco, and matches. They report extensive barter and black-market purchases, severe enforcement, adulterated or substituted foods, inadequate restaurant meals, and periods when families went hungry. Clothing coupons, soap, shoes, umbrellas, towels, socks, and work clothes were also sharply restricted, with corruption sometimes preventing laborers from receiving their allotments. The transcript continues beyond page 56.
